Abstract
Integrating LLMs with automated writing evaluation can transform
scoring models into feedback tutors that translate diagnostic signals
into actionable guidance. Ensuring reliable and consistent results
in such systems requires addressing information overload, yet they
still rely on manual intervention to extract key signals for meaning-
ful feedback, limiting full automation. To address these challenges,
we propose FEAK, a pipeline for Korean writing that dynamically

identifies rubric-linked linguistic features with low values and uses
them as evidence for LLM-based feedback generation. By ground-
ing generative feedback in measurable diagnostic signals, FEAK
generates interpretable and verifiable feedback. This design bridges
quantitative evaluation with pedagogically meaningful guidance
while operating autonomously. Experiments with automatic and
human evaluations show that FEAK generates real-time feedback
comparable to expert guidance and outperforms general LLM-based
systems in quality and reliability.

1
Introduction
The goal of writing instruction is to help learners express their
thoughts clearly and logically [11]. Formative feedback is widely
recognized as the most effective means of achieving this goal [13].
However, in real world educational settings, providing consistent,
timely, and specific feedback to all learners remains structurally
difficult [9]. To address this challenge, extensive research has been
conducted on Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) systems [30].
Traditional AWE systems achieve high scoring accuracy by lever-
aging interpretable linguistic features such as lexical diversity and
syntactic complexity [24]. Nevertheless, they largely function as
sophisticated graders rather than tutors, as they fail to translate
diagnostic results into actionable, sentence-level feedback that ef-
fectively supports revision. To bridge this diagnosis-to-action gap,
recent studies have begun integrating large language models (LLMs)
to generate feedback beyond simple grading.
Despite their generative capabilities, existing LLM-based feed-
back approaches face fundamental limitations. Methods that rely
solely on rubric scores and original texts tend to produce overly
general or inconsistent feedback, while incorporating all linguistic
features at once leads to information overload and reduced reli-
ability due to excessive input length. As a result, many systems
still depend on human intervention to identify and prioritize key
feedback signals, undermining the goal of fully automated feedback.
Furthermore, most prior work has focused on English, leaving a
substantial gap for languages with complex morphology such as
Korean. Directly applying English centric models often fails to cap-
ture the linguistic and discourse-level nuances of Korean writing,
highlighting the need for a language-specific approach.
To address these challenges, particularly in the context of Korean
writing education, we propose FEAK (Feature-based Evaluation
and AI feedback for Korean writing). FEAK dynamically identifies
rubric-linked linguistic features with significantly low values and
uses them as explicit evidence for LLM-based feedback generation.
By grounding generative feedback in measurable diagnostic signals,
FEAK ensures that each suggestion is interpretable, verifiable, and
pedagogically meaningful, effectively integrating AWE’s robust
quantitative assessment with the generative strengths of LLMs.
FEAK operates in three stages. First, an enhanced AWE model
analyzes the input essay to compute linguistic features and rubric
scores (Evaluation stage, Section 3.1). Next, these features are
compared against elite benchmark data to dynamically select rubric-
relevant features that exhibit the largest deficiencies (Feature Ex-
traction stage, Section 3.2). Finally, FEAK generates sentence-level
feedback using a concise evidence sheet containing the selected
feature values and their standardized gaps from benchmark distri-
butions (Feedback stage, Section 3.3). Both automatic and human
evaluations demonstrate that FEAK produces real-time feedback
comparable to expert guidance while outperforming general LLM-
based systems in quality and reliability.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We propose FEAK, a framework for Korean writing that effec-
tively integrates a refined AWE system with an LLM to bridge the
gap between quantitative evaluation and generative feedback.
• FEAK dynamically selects priority linguistic features by com-
paring the current essay with elite benchmark data, enabling
focused and adaptive feedback generation while reducing the
need for external intervention.
• Experiments show that FEAK generates real-time feedback com-
parable to expert guidance, outperforming general LLM-based
systems in both quality and reliability.
2
Related Work
In this section, we first review the evolution of AWE systems (Sec-
tion 2.1). Next, we examine LLM-based feedback approaches, em-
phasizing emerging requirements: i) Explainable grounding, ii) Dy-
namic selection, and iii) Autonomous operation (Section 2.2). We
finally review Korean feedback systems through these perspectives,
highlighting their current challenges and gaps (Section 2.3).
2.1
Automated Writing Evaluation
Automated writing evaluation (AWE) has evolved through various
scoring systems and methods. Early systems [18, 10, 3] quantified
writing quality with interpretable features derived from linguistic
indicators and coupled them with predictive models. Subsequently,
deep learning models [30, 8, 33] and pre-trained language models
[34, 32, 22] advanced scoring performance. Recent AWE research
has improved the accuracy and generalization of automated essay
scoring through advances in neural and feature-based modeling.
UKTA [2] provides a unified Korean AWE framework that con-
nects morpheme, feature, and rubric processing while reducing
error propagation introduced by a Korean-specific morphological
analyzer. [7] improved representation and generalization by com-
bining grammatical diversity with error signals as auxiliary tasks
in a multitask learning setup, while calibrating the scoring function

with IRT. PLAES [5] employs a level-aware representation learn-
ing framework that enhances robustness to prompt variation and
promotes cross-prompt generalization.
2.2
LLM-based Writing Feedback
The emergence of LLMs has shifted automated writing educa-
tion from static evaluation to dynamic feedback [14]. Recent work
demonstrates the educational effectiveness of LLM-based feedback
and focuses on improving its quality and instructional value [6, 14].
In parallel, a line of research emphasizes reliability and evidence-
based feedback [28]. In educational contexts, feedback is only mean-
ingful when students can understand and trust it [15], a princi-
ple that aligns with Explainable AI (XAI), which aims to make
AI decision-making processes transparent [1]. Motivated by this,
SWIF2T [4] demonstrated the importance of explainable grounding
by leveraging Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to generate
feedback based on objective facts from external scientific literature.
Another major research stream concerns the prioritization of
feedback. [26] noted that while LLMs excel at local suggestions,
they often overlook global issues like logical flaws in an entire text.
Similarly, the Lost in the Middle phenomenon [23] highlighted the
limitations of processing long contexts. Both studies underscore the
need for feedback systems to dynamically identify and prioritize
the most important features for improvement.
Finally, research aimed at securing the practicality and stabil-
ity of feedback systems is also active. The issue of inconsistent
LLM outputs poses a significant barrier to practical application
[31]. PROF [25] introduced a dual LLM framework with a feedback
generator and a student simulator, proposing a novel training loop
that directly optimizes feedback performance through simulated
learner revisions. This demonstrates that autonomous operation
with minimal external intervention is a crucial system requirement.
In sum, the core requirements for the current generation of LLM-
based feedback systems converge on three principles: explainable
grounding, dynamic selection, and autonomous operation.
2.3
LLM-based Korean Writing Feedback
While the above requirements—explainable grounding, dynamic
selection, and autonomous operation—are well studied in English-
dominant contexts, Korean writing education presents distinct chal-
lenges. Korean’s agglutinative morphology and complex discourse
patterns complicate linguistic feature extraction, making accurate
diagnosis more difficult than in English [2].
In Korea, the adoption of commercial LLM-based writing feed-
back services is rapidly increasing for use in educational settings
[17]. KEEWiT1 provides evaluation and feedback across six rubrics
based on predefined foundational features such as essay length,
paragraph structure, and orthography. Jajakjajak2 integrates rubric-
based AI writing evaluation into the classroom workflow, while
CLIPPO3 analyzes student writing based on grade level, subject-
specific, or teacher-customized criteria to generate personalized
feedback reports. While Korean commercial services offer practical

In contrast to the rapid growth of commercial services, Korean

[2]. Consequently, a systematic framework that satisfies these re-

3
Methodology

Evaluation and AI feedback for Korean writing). FEAK inte-
grates quantitative diagnosis with evidence-grounded generation to

tonomous operation. Figure 3 demonstrates the complete pipeline
through an example. The Evaluation stage (Section 3.1) computes

The Feedback stage (Section 3.3) translates these objective diagnos-

3.1
Enhanced AWE Architecture
This section describes the enhanced AWE architecture, which quan-
tifies linguistic features and rubric scores to provide interpretable
diagnostic signals for feedback generation.
The Evaluation stage computes 29 linguistic features and 8 rubric
scores from the input essay. This stage builds upon [2] but is re-
trained on a subset of 29 features, retained from the original 294 to
keep only the most relevant signals for the downstream dynamic
prioritization. The selection criteria are detailed in Section 3.2.1.
Key enhancements include expanded token capacity from 50 to
200, mean pooling over BiGRU hidden states, replacing the final-
state representation, and Content-Grounded Contextual Attention
that dynamically weights features based on essay semantics. The
internal architecture is illustrated in Figure 2.
Given an essay with 𝑁sentences, pre-trained KoBERT4 encodes
each sentence and a bidirectional GRU processes the sequence.
The 𝑑-dimensional essay representation h ∈R𝑑is obtained by
mean-pooling all hidden states followed by layer normalization.
Simultaneously, 29 critical linguistic features f ∈R29 are computed
via rule-based algorithms on morphologically analyzed text. These
features include ending diversity, type-token ratios, and sentence
overlap measures.
4https://github.com/SKTBrain/KoBERT
Evaluation stage then computes content-aware feature weights
via contextual attention:
𝜶FEAK = softmax(Wattnh + battn)
(1)
where Wattn and battn are learnable attention parameters. Un-
like prior models with fixed weights [2], these attention weights
𝜶FEAK ∈R29 adapt to each essay’s content, indicating which fea-
tures are most salient for scoring this specific essay. Using these
attention weights, the weighted features undergo linear projection
and are concatenated with the essay representation:
hfinal = [h ; Wproj(𝜶FEAK ⊙f)]
(2)
Finally, this integrated vector is passed to a fully-connected layer
to produce rubric scores:
s = Wouthfinal + bout
(3)
where s ∈R8 contains scores for eight evaluation rubrics: Topic
Clarity, Narrative Quality, Originality, Intra-paragraph Structure,
Inter-paragraph Structure, Grammar, Vocabulary, and Sentence
Expression.
The evaluation stage outputs three components used in subse-
quent stages: feature values f ∈R29, rubric scores s ∈R8, and
Content-Grounded Contextual Attention weights 𝜶FEAK ∈R29.
The high accuracy of this content-aware scoring model ensures
the reliability of the subsequent diagnoses by the Feature Extrac-
tion and Feedback stages. The attention weights are reused by the
Selector to prioritize features that are both statistically deficient
via elite gap analysis and contextually salient for this essay.

3.2
Diagnostic-based Feature Extraction
This stage compares the linguistic feature scores of the current
essay against elite benchmarks and dynamically identifies the core
features most likely to yield the largest improvements in writing
quality. By focusing on a small set of priority features, this stage
filters out redundant information and concentrates the model’s
attention on the most interpretable signals for feedback generation,
enhancing both clarity and reliability in the subsequent process.
3.2.1
Offline Core Feature Selection and Elite Benchmarking. Prior
to deployment, we selected 29 core features from the full set of 294
by balancing diagnostic power with interpretability. This offline
reduction removes highly correlated or redundant features and re-
duces computational cost, resulting in a cleaner and more coherent
semantic space for reliable downstream selection.
The initial candidate pool was proposed in consultation with Ko-
rean linguistics experts and validated via five statistical procedures:
(1) Univariate correlation significance (Pearson/Spearman)
(2) Multivariate OLS significance (VIF filtering, HC3-robust)
(3) Lasso stable selection (frequency ≥0.6)
(4) Mutual information (top 25%)
(5) Permutation importance (top 25%)
Features satisfying at least three criteria were reviewed by ex-
perts, yielding 29 final features. These selected features are grouped
into six highly reliable dimensions for Korean writing assessment,
as shown in Table 1.
To enable relative evaluation, FEAK compares each essay’s fea-
ture scores against elite benchmarks derived from the top 10% of
high-scoring essays. For each feature we computed and stored the
elite mean 𝜇elite, standard deviation 𝜎elite, and decile values. The
deciles serve as qualitative thresholds for interpreting feature states
such as Lacking, Adequate, or Excessive. The set of 29 selected
core features and their elite benchmarks are built offline prior to
system deployment. The dynamic feature selection procedure for
new essays is described in the next section.
3.2.2
Dynamic Feature Selection. Dynamic Feature Selector dy-
namically identifies six of the 29 features most likely to improve the
essay through a three-step process: (1) detecting the lowest-scoring
rubrics, (2) measuring each feature’s deviation from elite bench-
marks, and (3) ranking features by gap size, attention weight, and
need for improvement to select the top six for feedback generation.
• Step 1: Identify the two lowest-scoring rubrics. The system
selects the two lowest rubrics among the eight rubric scores pro-
duced by the Analyzer. For example, a low Sentence Expression
score suggests issues with sentence-level fluency or variation.
• Step 2: Quantify elite gaps for the 29 features. For each core
feature, the system computes a normalized deviation:

The three components represent gap magnitude, model salience,

After scoring, we perform rubric-balanced selection targeting
the two lowest scoring rubrics identified in Step 1. For each rubric,
we use a pre-defined expert-mapped feature set from the offline
setup. For example, Sentence Expression maps to features including
ending diversity and average sentence length. We then select the
top three features by priority score within each set. If fewer than
six total are obtained, we take replacement from the global ranking.
This process yields up to six features, three per low-scoring
rubric. Crucially, the Selector does not enumerate all features but
dynamically chooses only those mapped to the essay’s vulnerable
rubrics. In this way, the system quantitatively determines which
rubric, which feature, and by how much each should be improved.
• Final output. The system produces a structured evidence sheet
containing the selected features and diagnostic metadata: current
value, elite mean, z-score, qualitative status, target rubric, and
expert guidelines. This evidence sheet then serves as the input
to the feedback stage (see Figure 3).
These explicit justifications distinguish our approach from sys-
tems that report only rubric scores. A bare score like 2 out of 6
only signals weakness, whereas the evidence sheet provides con-
crete metrics (e.g., ending diversity notably below the elite average)„
enabling the feedback to produce verifiable guidance.

3.3
Evidence-Based Feedback Generation
The Feedback stage transforms the selected outputs into sentence-
level feedback that students can understand and act upon. It receives
six features, two weak rubrics, and the structured evidence sheet
from the previous stage. The core design principle of the Feedback
stage is to constrain the LLM to act as a translator rather than
an evaluator. If the LLM were given the entire essay and asked to
identify problems and generate feedback freely, it could hallucinate
nonexistent issues or misjudge their importance. Instead, the stage
uses the objective measurements computed in Section 3.1 and the
selected features from Section 3.2 as explicit constraints, effectively
narrowing the generation scope.
3.3.1
Constrained Prompting. The prompt combines three inputs:
the original essay with numbered sentences, the two lowest rubrics
identified in Step 1, and the evidence sheet for the selected six
features. This structure is shown in the Generator input of Figure 3.
The prompt includes explicit instructions. First, locate the text
segment showing the largest rubric-feature gap. Second, for that
segment, generate feedback that moves the feature toward the elite
mean and raises the rubric score. Third, all numerical values must be
reproduced exactly as provided, without modification or inference.
The LLM leverages its surface-level pattern recognition capabil-
ity. For example, if ending diversity is diagnosed as low, the Genera-
tor can detect repeated sentence-final endings without performing
morphological analysis and cite those sentences as evidence. By
separating evaluation from feedback generation, each feedback
instance becomes auditable and traceable to quantitative evidence.
3.3.2
Three-Part Feedback Structure. Figure 1 illustrates a real ex-
ample of FEAK’s output interface, showing how the system converts
an input essay into rubric-level evaluations and concrete sentence-
level feedback. (A) displays the original essay with highlighted
evidence sentences, (B) presents rubric scores across eight evalua-
tion dimensions, and (C) shows the generated feedback containing
evidence-linked suggestions and revision examples.
The generated feedback consists of three parts. The Phenom-
enon section explains what the problem is and why it matters,
linking feature measurements to readability or rhetorical effective-
ness. The Evidence section cites specific sentences by number that
demonstrate the problem. The Revision section provides concrete
before-and-after examples. Figure 3 presents an illustrative example
of this structure, showing how the overall pipeline operates for a
single feedback instance.
This structure separates diagnosis from prescription, ensuring
that students first understand the problem before seeing the solu-
tion. Although the visible feedback appears concise and natural,
each piece of advice is grounded in an extensive internal reason-
ing chain. Every suggestion can be traced through the Analyzer’s
feature computations, the Selector’s elite-gap comparisons and z-
scores, and the evidence constraints embedded in the Generator.
Internally, all feature values and elite distributions are fully stored,
allowing quantitative verification of every generated comment.
For example, while the student only sees user-friendly feed-
back such as “Vary your sentence endings for better flow,” the sys-
tem internally refers to quantitative indicators such as the ending-
diversity score (4.3) and the corresponding z-score (2.33) relative
to the elite benchmark. These values, along with corresponding
entries in the evidence sheet, form the factual basis that supports
each piece of feedback.
Overall, this pipeline bridges the gap between quantitative eval-
uation and meaningful feedback, integrating measurable linguistic
evidence with controlled generation to produce feedback that is
both interpretable and pedagogically meaningful.
4
Experiments
We evaluate FEAK through both user-based and model-based exper-
iments to assess its effectiveness and reliability in real educational
contexts. Specifically, we investigate the following research ques-
tions (RQs):
• RQ1: Does FEAK’s evidence-based feedback improve writing
quality compared to expert feedback and LLM feedback?
• RQ2: How do users perceive FEAK’s feedback in terms of use-
fulness, specificity, trustworthiness, evidence alignment, and
satisfaction?
• RQ3: Does the enhanced Analyzer achieve higher scoring per-
formance than the baseline model?
4.1
Experimental Settings
To address the research questions, we conducted two experiments: a
user feedback study (RQ1, RQ2) evaluating FEAK’s feedback quality
and educational impact, and a model evaluation (RQ3) assessing
the model’s accuracy and reliability.
4.1.1
User Feedback Experiment (RQ1, RQ2).
• Participants. We recruited 21 undergraduate students majoring
in engineering and randomly assigned them to three conditions:
Expert feedback, FEAK feedback, and general-purpose LLM feed-
back, with approximately seven participants per condition.
• Task. All participants were asked to write an argumentative es-
say on the topic “My good deed and what I learned from it”, which
was selected from the Korean high school writing curriculum.
Using a single topic controlled for potential topic effects.
• Procedure. Each participant completed three stages in sequence:
draft writing (15 minutes), feedback review (5 minutes), and
revision (10 minutes). The total duration and sequence were
identical across all conditions to ensure comparability.
• Feedback Generation. We controlled the feedback format, num-
ber of items (maximum three), and exposure duration across all
conditions. All feedback was generated with temperature set to
0.2, top-𝑝to 0.9, and a maximum generation length of 512 tokens
for consistency across conditions.
– Expert feedback: Produced by a Korean language education
specialist and served as the human upper bound.
– LLM feedback: Generated by GPT-4o-mini using the same
constrained prompt template as FEAK, serving as the baseline
condition.

4.1.2
Model Performance Evaluation (RQ3). To validate the en-
hanced Analyzer, we used the AI-HUB5 Essay Evaluation Dataset
containing approximately 46,000 Korean essays from elementary
to high school students, each scored by experts on 8 rubrics. We
used 40,000 essays for training and 6,000 for testing. Evaluation
metrics included Accuracy and Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK).
The baseline for performance comparison was the UKTA model [2],
which was reproduced under the same data and evaluation settings
to ensure fairness.
4.2
Experimental Results
4.2.1
Feedback Quality and Efficiency (RQ1). Table 2 presents the
quality improvements across feedback conditions. FEAK achieved
5https://www.aihub.or.kr/
an average improvement of +4.43 points, which was not signifi-
cantly different from expert feedback (+5.43 points, 𝑝= .231) but
significantly higher than the general-purpose LLM (+2.14 points,
𝑝= .028). A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of
feedback type on writing improvement (𝐹(2, 18) = 6.42, 𝑝= .008,
𝜂2 = .42). Tukey’s post-hoc test confirmed that both expert and
FEAK feedback produced significantly greater gains than the LLM
condition (Expert vs. LLM: 𝑝= .006; FEAK vs. LLM: 𝑝= .028),
whereas the difference between Expert and FEAK was not statisti-
cally significant.
In terms of efficiency, FEAK generated feedback in an average of
16.4 seconds per essay, approximately 25 times faster than human
experts (471 seconds) while maintaining comparable quality. Al-
though the general-purpose LLM provided the fastest response
(8.8 seconds), its improvement effect was substantially smaller.
These results indicate that FEAK achieves near-expert feedback
quality with dramatically higher efficiency, suggesting strong poten-
tial as a practical and scalable solution for real educational settings.
4.2.2
User Perception (RQ2). Table 3 presents user ratings across
five perception dimensions. Expert feedback received the highest
overall ratings, especially in specificity and trustworthiness, which
may reflect its more detailed and context-sensitive nature. FEAK
feedback was rated moderately high, outperforming the general-
purpose LLM in all dimensions, especially in evidence alignment
and usefulness, where participants appreciated the clarity of its
explanations. The general-purpose LLM feedback received lower
overall ratings, though its satisfaction score was relatively higher,
likely due to its brevity and readability. Overall, these results in-
dicate that FEAK provides concrete, evidence-based feedback that
users perceive as informative, reliable, and pedagogically useful.
4.2.3
Analyzer Performance (RQ3). Table 4 compares the enhanced
Analyzer against the baseline UKTA model. The enhanced ver-
sion improved Accuracy on 6 of 8 rubrics and QWK on 6 of 8
rubrics. Substantial improvements were observed in the Content
category (Topic Clarity, Originality, Narrative) and Organization
category (Inter-paragraph Structure). Overall, Accuracy improved
from 0.642 to 0.655 (+1.3pp) and QWK from 0.474 to 0.521 (+4.7pp).
These improvements demonstrate that architectural enhancements
including mean pooling, layer normalization, and content-aware
attention positively impact rubric scoring accuracy. Reliable diag-
nostics are essential for downstream stages, as inaccurate scoring
would propagate errors through the entire pipeline.
5
Conclusion
We introduced FEAK, a pipeline that bridges the diagnosis-to-action
gap by integrating interpretable feature-based diagnosis with con-
strained LLM generation. The system comprises three stages: an
enhanced Analyzer computing linguistic features and rubric scores,
a dynamic Selector prioritizing key features through statistical
comparison, and a constrained Generator producing sentence-level
feedback grounded in verifiable evidence. Experiments with 21 par-
ticipants demonstrate that FEAK achieves quality improvements
comparable to expert feedback while being faster and markedly
outperforming general-purpose LLMs. Future research will address
